full_judgment:
A.F.M. Abdur Rahman, J: Under Article 102 of the Constitution the petitioner, Appollo Ispat Complex Limited, obtained the instant Rule Nisi calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order issued under Memo No. 5(13)98/Cus-Bond/Lice/2005/14283 dated 18.7.2005 (Annexure B) refusing to grant bonded ware house licence to the petitioner should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and also to show cause as to why the respondents should not be directed to issue a bonded warehouse license to the petitioner as prayed for and/or pass such other or further order or order as to this Court may deem fit and proper.

2. Petitioner is a private limited company incorporated under Companies Act, 1994 and duly registered with the Board of Investment, Government of Bangladesh. The petitioner is engaged, through its C.R.Coil manufacturing unit, in the business of manufacturing C.R.Coil (Cold rolls coil) from raw materials of H. R. Coils, (Hot rolled coil) and is now one of the leading manufacturer in Bangladesh employing over 400 workers with working capital of Taka 100 cores. The petitioner produces about 6000 mertic tons of C.R.Coil per month and has the capacity to produce around 1,20,000 metric tons per annum. The petitioner is required to import raw materials particularly H. R. Coils from abroad regularly. The petitioner is aggrieved by a decision issued under Memo No. 5(13)98/cus-bond/lice/2005/14283 dated 18.7.2005 issued by the respondent No. 4 on behalf of the respondent No.3 purporting to reject the petitioner application praying for a bonded ware-house licence on the ground that there is no scope for allowing any new bond licence facilities for home consumption giving an existing government decision to this effect.

3. It has further been asserted by the petitioner that the Respondent No. 2 on 18.3.2003 issued an order withdrawing bonded ware-house licence facilities from 18 different industrial sector for the purpose of securing immediate revenues and for protection of domestic industries, including industries manufacturing G. P. sheets and C. I. sheets. The petitioner asserted that the said order did not include industries producing C.R. Coils. Moreover; the said order was not issued by way of a notification in the Official Gazette. Despite the facts of issuance of such order dated 18.3.2003 the respondent No. 3 in the exercise of its power under Section 13 of the Customs Act, 1969 has continued to grant bonded warehouse licence to industries which are not included in the aforesaid 18 sectors for which such facilities have been withdrawn. In particular the Respondent No.3 has granted such licence in favour of four competitor industries of the petitioner company, all of which are enjoying bonded warehouse facilities for importing as raw materials H.R. Coils for the purpose of manufacture of C.R.Coils namely M/S KY C.R Coils mills limited of Kumuria, Chittagong, PHP Steel Mills Ltd. of Kumuria, Chittagong, S.Alam Cold Roll Steel Mills Limited, Sitakundo, Chittagong and Abul Khair Cold Roll Steel Mills Limited, Sitakundo, Chittagong.

4. The petitioner further asserted that the petitioner company duly applied on 15.05.2005 in the prescribed form to the respondent No, 2 praying for issuance of a private bonded warehouse license to enable it to store huge quantity imported raw materials in the bonded warehouse without being required to pay taxes and duties immediately upon arrival of the said raw materials. In the absence of a bonded warehouse license the petitioner is required to divert a substantial part of its working capital for the payment of customs duties and taxes on each occasion that a consignment of raw materials is imported into the country for the purpose of production. The petitioner had fulfilled all the conditions of prevailing of practice provided under Section 13 of the Customs Act, 1969 for the granting of a bonded warehouse licence including the submission of all relevant supporting documentation as required by the Respondent No. 2 for granting applications for such licences made under Section 13 of the Act, which included, among others,. its trade license, import registration certificate, VAT Registration Certificate, TIN Certificate, Bank Solvency Certificate, Bonds executed for Taka 40 crores by all of the petitioner Company's Di-rectors and a letter under Memo No. Sho:-2/05/679 dated 30.4.2005 issued by the Board of Investment and addressed to the respondent No.2 expressly recommending that the petitioner company be granted a bonded warehouse licence subject to certain criteria being met. On 13.6.2005 the Respondent No.3 Commissioner of Customs (Bond) sent a letter to the Member, National Board of Revenue, Respondent No 2, under Memo No. 5(13)98/cus-bond/lice/2005/11507 wherein it has been admitted that the petitioner is entitled to the issuance of bonded warehouse licence confirming that the goods produced by the petitioner company were not included in the list of 18 sectors industries from which bonded warehouse facilities has

been withdrawn pursuant to the Board's earlier order dated 18.3.2003 and further confirming that the petitioner company is producing C.R. Coil against four competitors to which bonded warehouse facility have been granted and that the Board of Investment has recommended that the petitioner company be granted a bonded warehouse licence and also confirmed that the petitioner company has observed all the legal requirements and submitted necessary documents in support of its application. The petitioner categorically asserted that the Respondent No. 3 sent the said letter to the Respondent No.2 in abdication of his power under Section 13(1) of the Customs Act, 1969 and prayed for a direction from the National Board of Revenue. On 12.7.2005 the Respondent No. 2 by a letter issued under Memo No. 1(1) Customs: Export and Bond/99/262 issued by the Second Secretary (Customs Export and Bond), NBR addressed to the respondent No. 3 in response to the letter dated 13.6.2005, referring to a government decision that no new bond facilities will be provided for home consumption and that such existing bond facilities will be withdrawn from all sector and requested the Respondent No 3 that information be provided by the Respondent No. 3 regarding steps taken to withdraw bond facilities from the 18 sector of industries in pursuance of the letter dated 18.3.2005. Thereafter the Respondent No. 3 issued the impugned letter to the petitioner refusing to grant bonded warehouse licence in favour of the petitioner. Petitioner challenging the said refusal preferred this petition and obtained the Rule Nisi.

5. In pursuance of the Rule, which has duly been served upon the respondents, learned Deputy Attorney General Mrs. Syeda Afsar Jahan along with learned Assistant Attorney General Mr. Shafiul Alam Mahmood appeared on behalf of the respondents and preferred affidavit-in-opposition on behalf of the Respondent No. 3.

6. It has been asserted by the Respondent No.3 that in exercise of powers as conferred by Section 13(2) of the Customs Act, 1969 National Board of Revenue imposed prohibition on issuance of bond licence in respect of home consumption of different industrial raw materials and different 18 sectors industries have been included in such prohibition. The government further formulated policy for withdrawing the existing bonded warehouse facilities from all sectors of industry and has directed the customs authority to refuse any prayer for issuance of bond licence over and above these 18 sectors as provided earlier in the policy formulation. The Respondent No. 3 further asserted that it being the subordinate to the National Board of Revenue can not exercise his discretionary power under Section 13 of the Customs Act 1969 in respect of issuance of bond licence without the approval of the National Board of Revenue and as such the refusal made on the application of the petitioner praying for issuance of bond licence in pursuance of the direction of Respondent No.2 is lawful.

7. Mr. Salahuddin Ahmed along with Ms. Sara Hossain and Mr. Ramzan Ali Sikder conducted the hearing on behalf of the petitioner before this Court while learned Deputy Attorney General Mrs. Syeda Afsar Jahan along with learned Assistant Attorney General Mr. Shafiul Alam Mahmood conducted the hearing on behalf of the Respondents.

8. We have heard the learned Advocates, perused the petition, affidavit-in-opposition, the supplementary affidavit filed by the petitioner and the Annexures appended thereto. We have also perused the up-to-date legal position and considered the argument advanced at the bar at its true perspective.

9. The petitioner, a private limited company having been registered by the Board of Investment as C.R. Coil Manufacturing Industries holds import licence for import of raw materials including H. R.Coils, made an application to the customs authority praying for granting the facilities of bonded warehouse licence under the provision of Section 13 of the Customs Act, 1969 and having been refused, allegedly arbitrarily, assailed, the decision of refusal, Annexure-B, and has taken mainly two grounds of objection.

10. In substantiating the first ground of objection, Mr. Salahuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, has taken us to the recent amendment of Section 13 of the Customs Act, 1969 and argued that the National Board of Revenue pursuant to the amended provision has not yet formulated and imposed any condition, limitation and restriction on the granting of bonded warehouse licence for private warehouses and the petitioner having fulfilled all the requirements prevailing at the time, upon which the Respondent No.3 already granted licence to other competitors of the petitioner, the respondents are duty bound to grant bond licence to the petitioner on the usual terms and conditions as per prevailing practice.

11. Mr. Salahuddin. Ahmed after taking us through the Annexure-G and H strenuously argued that Respondent No. 3 since empowered under Section 13(1) of the Customs Act, 1969 for granting bond licence to a applicant must consider to exercise his discretion upon the application objectively on its own merits and in exercising such discretion ought not to rely upon any extraneous direction.

12. Mr. Ahmed in maintaining his first ground of objection further taken us to Annexure-C and vigorously argued that the Respondent No. 2 National Board of Revenue, though arbitrarily decided to withdraw bonded warehouse licence facilities from 18 category of industries, yet the C.R. Coil Manufacturing Sector has not been included within that decision and as such the respondents are not entitled to refuse bond licence to the petitioner.

13. Mr. Salahuddin Ahmed further contends that so long the statutory provision of Section 13(2) of the Customs Act 1969 in respect of granting bond licence to private warehouse exist in the present formulation, the respondent No. 3 can not abdicate his power to the Respondent No. 2 on the plea of control under Section 4 of Customs Act 1969 and must exercise its discretion in favour of the applicant who fulfilled the requirement of prevailing practice. Mr. Ahmed categorically pointed that the petitioner since, under all circumstances, is admittedly entitled to the bonded warehouse licence, the Respondent No. 3 is duty bond to exercise his discretion in favour of the petitioner.

14. The bone contention of the petitioner lies in the fact that Section 13 of the Customs Act, 1969 empowered Respondent No. 3 to exercise discretion in granting bonded ware-house licence to industries allowing an opportunity not to pay immediately the Customs and other duties and to maintain private ware-house for the purpose of storing imported raw materials and the petitioner having fulfilled all the requirements under the prevailing practice was admittedly entitled to such exercise of discretion in his favour but the respondent No. 3 abdicated his such power to the Respondent No. 2, National Board of Revenue, who arbitrarily made a policy decision to withdraw bonded warehouses licence from 18 category of industrial concern and the petitioner not being in those 18 category of industrial concern have been arbitrarily refused mainly by the respondent No.2 to grant bonded ware-house licence on the basis of the said policy formulation.

15. Before appreciating this contention of the petitioner the present provision of Section 13 of the Customs Act, 1969 may profitably be quoted which is a amended version of the original Section 13 which came into effect on and from 01.7.2003 through Finance Act, 2003. The amended version of Section 13 of the Customs Act runs as follows:-

13. Licensing of private warehouses- (1) Subject to sub-section (2) at any ware-housing station, the Commissioner of Customs (Bond) or any other Commissioner of Customs authorized by the Board may licence private warehouses wherein dutiable goods imported by or on behalf of the licensee, or any other imported goods in respect of which facilities for deposit in a public warehouse are not available, may be deposited. (2) The Board may, from time to time, by notification in the official Gazette, impose conditions, limitations or restrictions-

(a) on granting licence for private warehouse:

(b) on goods to be warehoused ; and

(c) on import entitlement of the ware-house.

(3) The Commissioner of Customs (Bond) of any other Commissioner of Customs authorized by the Board may, suspend or cancel a licence granted under sub-section (1)-

(a) if the licensee contravenes any provision of this Act or the rules made thereunder or commits breach of any of the conditions of the licence; or .

(b) in the case where, he deems fit, a license to be suspended or can-celled in the public interest: Provided that in case of cancellation of any licensee, the licensee shall be served with a show cause notice of thirty days, and be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard."

16. From bare reading of the provision of Section 13 of the Customs Act, 1969 the discretion of the customs authority in granting bonded ware house licence, to be exercised through Respondent No. 3, Commissioner of Customs (Bond), apparently reveals out from the word "May" occurring in sub section 1 of Section 13 of the Customs Act, 1969. The learned Deputy Attorney General Mrs. Syeda Afsar Jahan relying upon the word "May" as aforesaid categorically submits that the petitioner has no legal right to compel the customs authority to exercise the discretion in his favour. The learned Deputy Attorney General further contends that the customs authorities are under the general Administration and Control of the National Board of Revenue for which the Customs Authorities are duty bound by any policy formulation made by the National Board of Revenue and be that Customs authority is satisfied with the fulfillment of the requirements by the petitioner regarding the application method, yet it can not exercise its discretion in favour of granting bonded warehouse licence overriding the policy decision of the National Board of Revenue which policy normally has the approval of the government. The learned Deputy Attorney General in favour of her contention regarding policy formulation and its binding effect referred to Annexure-C appended to the writ petition and cited the decision of S.A. Coconut Oil Mills Ltd —Vs- Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh reported in 54 DLR-1.

Control of National Board of Revenue over the power and function of the Customs authority under the Customs Act, 1969 have been provided under Section 4 of the Customs Act, 1969 which runs as follows:-

"4. Powers and duties of officer of Customs- An officer of Customs appointed under section 3 shall exercise such powers and discharge such duties as are conferred or imposed on him by or under this Act; and he shall also be competent to exercise all powers and discharge all duties conferred or imposed upon any officer subordinate to him: Provided that, not withstanding anything contained in this Act or the rules, the Board may, by general or special order, impose such limitations or conditions on the exercise of such powers and dis-charge of such duties as it thinks fit."

17. From the cited decision it appears that a Division Bench of this Court in the case of S.A. Coconut Oil Mills Ltd. -vs- Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh reported in 54 DLR-1 while deciding the question of control of National Board of Revenue under the provisions of Section 4 of the Customs Act, 1969 upon the exercise of discretion of the customs authority, has held that.

"Section 4 of the Customs Act, 1969 thus provides for conferring a power upon an officer of the customs and the proviso to this section subjects him to the control of the National Board of Revenue which may exercise it by issuing a general or special order."

In paragraph 12 of the referred judgment it has further been observed by their lordship that; "

12. In deciding the applications for granting a warehouse licence under section 13 of the Customs Act, 1969 the Commissioner of Customs is guided and controlled by the policy adopted by the government for the granting of such licences."

18. We do not disagree that the customs authority in deciding the application praying for granting bonded warehouse licence is guided and control by the policy adopted by the government which may be exercised through National Board of Revenue as this provision was prevailing prior to amendment of Section 13 of Customs Act 1969. It appears that the question raised in this writ petition concerns the exercise of Power under Section 13 of the Customs Act 1969, admitting the general control of the National Board of Revenue upon the Customs authority, since a Specific power has been conferred upon the National Board of Revenue regarding imposition of control over the granting of Bonded Ware house licence by the Customs authority. But question remained whether the National Board of Revenue has yet imposed any such condition, limitation or restriction as provided by Section 13(2) of the Customs Act, 1969 and if imposed whether the National Board of Revenue has followed the mandatory procedure laid .down in the provision of law in promulgating such condition, limitation and restriction upon granting bonded Warehouse licence or that the Commissioner of Customs (Bond) is authorized to abdicate its power to the National Board of Revenue after imposition of such condition, limitation and restriction by the National Board of Revenue.

19. The petitioner, it appears from the writ petition, mainly framed its redress in the form of certiorari and mandamus in search of answer to these questions and prayed for a declaration as to the refusal to grant bonded warehouse licence as of without lawful authority and also prayed for directing the respondents to grant such licence in its favour.

20. It appears from a comprehensive reading of sub-section (1) & (2) of Section 13 of the Customs Act, 1969 that National Board of Revenue is empowered to impose conditions, limitations and restrictions amongst other, on the grant of bond licence to private warehouse by the Commissioner' of Customs (Bond) in exercise of his discretionary power but the said imposition of conditions limitations and restrictions must be notified in the official gazette. On our query the learned Deputy Attorney General frankly admits that the policy formulation upon which the alleged refusal relied upon has not yet been gazette notified or no conditions, limitations, and restrictions, has yet been gazette notified, apart from only making a policy formulation dated 18.10.2003, so as to make it an exercise under the provision of sub-section (2) of Section 13 of the Customs Act, 1969.

21. Annexure-H is the letter issued by 2nd Secretary (cus: export and bond) of National Board of Revenue on 12.7.2005 which directed the Commissioner of Customs (Bond), Respondent No.3 to refrain from issuing new bond licence for any category of industries which mentioned a circular issue from the National Board of Revenue under Memo No. ১(১) শুল্ক রপ্তানী ও বন্ড/৯৯/২০৩ তাং ১৮/৩/২০০৩ which has been annexed as Annexure-c to the writ petition. It appears from Annexure-c that National Board of Revenue has directed the Customs authority to act under the provision of section 13(2)(a) of the Customs Act, 1969 in cancelling bond licence facility of 18 categories industrial concern in which admittedly the petitioner does not fall. Annexure-C is reproduced here.

গণপ্রজাতন্ত্রী বাংলাদেশ সরকার

জাতীয় রাজস্ব বোর্ড

রাজস্ব ভবন, সেগুনবাগিচা, ঢাকা।

নথি নং- ১(১) শুল্কঃ রপ্তানি ও বন্ড/৯৯/২০৩(১)

তারিখঃ ১৮/০৩/২০০৩ খৃঃ

বিষয়ঃ রাজস্ব সংরক্ষন ও দেশজ শিল্পের প্রতিরক্ষনের স্বার্থে Home Consumption Bond ব্যবস্থাপনায় অধিকতর নিয়নন্ত্রন প্রতিষ্ঠাসহ কতিপয় শিল্পখাতে বন্ড সুবিধা প্রত্যাহার প্রসঙ্গে।

উর্পযুক্ত বিষয়ে দৃষ্টি আকর্ষন পূর্বক নির্দেশক্রমে জানানো যাচ্ছে যে, আমদানি-বিকল্প শিল্প বিকাশের লক্ষ্যে ইতোপূর্বে বিভিন্ন শিল্প খাতে ব্যাপক বন্ড সুবিধা প্রদান করা হয়েছিল। এই বন্ড সুবিধার অপব্যবহার হচ্ছে মর্মে নানা অভিযোগ রয়েছে। অধিকন্তু ইতোপূর্বে যে প্রেক্ষাপটে ও যেসব দিব বিবেচনায় এই ধরনের বন্ড লাইসেন্স প্রদান করা হয়েছিল সে প্রেক্ষাপট বর্তমানে পরিবর্তিত হয়েছে। এরুপ পরিবর্তিত পরিস্থিতিতে বাস্তব অবস্থা বিবেচনায় রাজস্ব সংরক্ষন ও দেশজ শিল্পের প্রতিরক্ষনের স্বার্থে যে খাতগুলোর সকল বন্ড লাইসেন্স প্রত্যাহার করা যায় তার বিস্তারিত তথ্য পর্যালোচনা ও সুপারিশ জাতীয় রাজস্ব বোর্ডে প্রেরণ করার জন্য কমিশনার, বন্ড কমিশনারেট, ঢাকা কে অনুরোধ জানানো হয়েছিল। উক্ত পত্রের প্রেক্ষিতে, বিদ্যমান Home Consumption Bond এর সংখ্যা, আমদানির পরিমান, রাজস্ব প্রাপ্তির পরিমান, বন্ডের আওতায় খালাসযোগ্য পণ্যের বর্তমান শুল্ক হার লাইসেন্স প্রাপ্ত প্রতিষ্ঠানের বন্ড কার্যক্রম, একই খাতে বন্ড সুবিধাবিহীন শিল্প প্রতিষ্ঠানের সংখ্যা ইত্যাদি দিক বিবেচনা করে বন্ড কমিশনারেট এর একটি প্রতিবেদন/সুপারিশ উক্ত দপ্তরের পত্র নং-৫(১৩)৬/বন্ড কমিঃ/কাস্টম শাখা/পলিসি/২০০১/২১৭৪৭ তারিখ ৩১/১২/২০০২ খৃঃ এর মাধ্যমে জাতীয় রাজস্ব বোর্ডে পাওয়া যায়। প্রাপ্ত প্রতিবেদন অনুযায়ী Home Consumption Bond সুবিধাভোগী ১৮টি খাত (যথাঃজি.পি শীট ও সি.আই.মীট, স্টীল ড্রাম, প্যাকেটকৃত গুড়াদুধ, কন্ডেসড মিল্ক, সরিষা ও নারকেল তৈল বৈদ্যুতিক পিটিংস ওয়েলডিং ইলেক্ট্রোডস কাগজ ও কাগজের বোর্ড দ্বারা তৈরি প্যাকিং সামগ্রী, কাগজ, কার্টন, পিপি ওভেন ব্যাগ, পলিয়েস্টার সুতা, মোটর গাড়ী, সিমেন্ট, মার্বেল ও গ্রানাইট স্লাব, ডিটারজেন্ট, নৌযান এবং এম.এস রড)এর অন্তর্ভুক্ত ৭০টি প্রতিষ্ঠানের বন্ড কার্যক্রম, প্রাপ্ত রাজস্বের পরিমাণ, একই খাতের বিদ্যমান বন্ড সুবিধা প্রাপ্ত ও বন্ড সুবিধাবিহীন প্রতিষ্ঠানের সংখ্যা ইত্যাদি দিক পরীক্ষা ও পর্যালোচনা করে দেখা হয়েছে। পর্যালোচনায় দেখা যায়যে, একদিকে বন্ড সুবিধার আfওতায় কোন কোন প্রতিষ্ঠান শুল্ককর পরিশোধ ব্যতিরেকে আমাদানিকৃত কাঁচামাল শুল্ক ষ্টেশন হতে খালাশ গ্রহন করেছে এবং অপরদিকে একই খাতের অন্য সকল প্রতিষ্ঠান শুল্ককর পরিশোধ করে আমদানিকৃত কাঁচামাল শুল্ক ষ্টেশন হতে খালাশ নিচ্ছে। ফলে, একই খাতের শিল্প প্রতিষ্ঠান সমূহের মধ্যে অসম প্রতিযোগিতা সৃষ্টি হচ্ছে। তাছাড়া, বন্ড সুবিধা প্রাপ্ত কোন কোন প্রতিষ্ঠানের আমাদনিযোগ্য কাঁচামাল দেশে উৎপাদিত হচ্ছে। দেশের স্বার্থে কাঁচামাল উৎপাদনকারী ঐ সকল প্রতিষ্ঠানের প্রতিরক্ষা  নিশ্চিত করা প্রয়োজন।

২। এখানে আরও উল্লেখ করা পয়োজন যে, ২০০২-২০০৩ অর্থ বছরের বাজেটে বন্ড সুবিধা সংকোচন ও নিয়ন্ত্রনের প্রস্তাব উপস্থাপিত হয়েছে। সেরকার গঠিত Revenue Reform Commission-কর্তৃক সম্প্রতি দাখিলকৃত Interim Report-এ এ বন্ডেড ওয়্যারহাউস পরিচালন, পরিবীক্ষন ও নিয়ন্ত্রণের ক্ষেত্রে নতুন নিয়ন্ত্রিত পদ্ধতি প্রণয়নের সুপারিশ পেশ করা হয়েছে।

৩। উপরি উক্ত প্রেক্ষাপটে রাজস্ব সংরক্ষন ও দেশীয় শিল্পের প্রতিরক্ষনের স্বার্থে অনুচ্ছেদ-০১ এ উল্লেখিত সকল প্রতিষ্ঠানের বন্ড সুবিধা প্রত্যাহার করা সহ কতিপয় ক্ষেত্রে অধিকতর নিয়ন্ত্রন আরোপ করা সমীচীন বিবেচনা করে সরকার নিম্নরূপ সিদ্ধান্ত গ্রহন করেছে, যথাঃ

(ক)অনুচ্ছেদ-০১ এ উল্রেখিত ১৮টি খাতভূক্ত সকল বন্ড লাইসেন্স বাতিলের লক্ষ্যে কমিশনার (বন্ড), ঢাকা, শুল্ক আইন, ১৯৬৯ এর ধারা ১৩(২) এর দফা (এ) অনুযায়ী আইনুনগ ব্যবস্থা গ্রহন করবেন। তবে, যে সকল প্রতিষ্ঠানের নিকট সরকারের বকেয়া পাওনা রয়েছে তাঁদের বন্ড লাইসেন্সগুলো প্রথমে সাময়িকভাবে বাতিল করে বকেয়া আদায় কার্যক্রম শেষে তা’ চূড়ান্তভাবে বাতিল করতে হবে।

(খ) অনুচ্ছেদ-১ এ উল্লেখিত ১৮(আঠার)টি শিল্প খাতে নতুন করে আর কোন Home Consumption বন্ড লাইসেন্স প্রদান করা হবে না;

(গ) অনিবার্য কোন কারনে উপরি উল্লিখিত ৭০টি প্রতিষ্ঠানের মধ্যে যাদের লাইসেন্স তাৎক্ষনিকভাবে বাতিলকরণ যতদিন পর্যন্ত সম্ভব হবে না, ততদিন পর্যন্ত ওস সকল প্রতিষ্ঠানের ক্ষেত্রে অন্তবর্তীকালীন ব্যবস্থা হিসাবে আমদানিকৃত কাঁচামালের উপর প্রযোজ্য শুল্ক/কর/ফি/চার্জ এর বিপরীতে নির্ধারিত ফরম-এ নিঃশর্ত ব্যাংক গ্যারান্টি গ্রহন পূর্বক শুল্ক আইন, ১৯৬৯ এর 86A অনুযায়ী পণ্য শুল্ক ভবন/ষ্টেশন হতে খালাস দেয়ার ব্যবস্থা নিতে হবে। উক্তরূপ বন্ড লাইসেন্স বাতিলকরণে ক্ষেত্রে বিদ্যমান অন্তরায় সমূহ দ্রুত অপসারণ করে অনুচ্ছেদ (ক) এ বির্ণত ব্যবস্থা গ্রহন করতে হবে,

(ঘ) এ ছাড়া Home Consumption  বন্ড সুবিধাপ্রাপ্ত অপরাপর খাতের সকল প্রতিষ্ঠানের ক্ষেত্রেও রাজস্ব সংরক্ষনকল্পে নিঃশর্ত ব্যাংকে গ্যরান্টি গ্রহন করে শুল্ক আইন ১৯৬৯ এর 86A ধারা অনুযায়ী আমদানী পণ্য খালাস দেয়ার ব্যবস্থা অবিলম্বে গ্রহন করতে হবে। তবে, মূল্য সংযোজন কর প্রাপ্তির প্রধান উৎসের কথা বিবেচনায় রেখে সিগারেট শিল্পের ক্ষেত্রে উক্তরূপ ব্যবস্থা প্রয়োগের বিষয়ে করণীয় সম্পর্কে পরবর্তীতে অবহিত করা হবে।

(ঙ) যেসব পণ্যের গুণগত মানের অবনতি ঘটার আশংকা থাকে- সেসব পণ্যের ক্ষেত্রে বল্ডিং মেয়াদ ৩(তিন), মাসের   অধিক নির্ধারণ না করার লক্ষ্যে শুল্ক আইন, ১৯৬৯ এর ধারা ৯৮(১)-তে প্রদত্ত ক্ষমতা প্রয়োগ করতে হবে।

০৪। কোন প্রতিষ্ঠানের ক্ষেত্রে অনুচ্ছেদ-০৩ এ বর্ণিত ব্যবস্থা কার্যকরণে মাননীয় উচ্চতর আদালত হতে উক্ত নিষেধাজ্ঞা/স্থগিতাদেশ এর বিপরীতে প্রতিবিধান গ্রহন করে সেমতে পরবর্তী ব্যবস্থা গ্রহন করতে হবে।

০৫। সরকারের উপরি উক্ত সিদ্ধান্ত সমূহ দ্রুত বাস্তবায়ন ও অনুসরণ করার জন্য নির্দেশক্রমে অনুরোধ জানানো হল।

22. This Annexure-C, as it appears, has 2 fold application, firstly, the Annexure-C does not impose any condition, limitation or restriction upon granting of bond licence by the Customs authority to all of or any category of industries, rather it simply explained the convenience and inconvenience of existing bond licence system concerning 18 categories of industries. Secondly it being only a letter from National Board of Revenue and not an instrument which is gazette notified, it can not achieve the status of a exercise under Section 13(2) of the Customs Act, 1969.

23. Therefore this Court can safely hold that the National Board of Revenue in exercise of power conferred by section 13(2) of the Customs Act, 1969 has not yet formulated and imposed any condition, limitation or restriction on the granting of bond licence to private warehouse and as such Annexure-C has no bearing upon the decision making process of the Respondent No 3 regarding grant of bond licence. Therefore the refusal to grant bonded warehouse licence relying on Annexure-C has no leg to stand and as such the same should be declared to have been made without lawful authority.

24. So far the question of abdication of Power by the respondent No.3 concerns, it appears that law empowered the Customs authority to exercise its discretion under Section 13(1) of the Customs Act 1969 subject to observing the condition, limitation and restriction imposed by the National Board of Revenue under the provision of Section 13(2) of the Customs Act 1969. Such a provision appears to have made the Customs authority independent from any further control by the National Board of Revenue on the matter of granting bonded ware house licence provided the National Board of Revenue has formulated and imposed such control and effected it through gazette notification. So long such specific imposition of control has not been made under the Provision of Section 13(2), the general control under Section 4 of the Customs act 1969 over the Customs authority shall be available to the National Board of Revenue as decided by their Lordships in the case of S.A. Coconut Oil Mills Limited -versus- Government of Bangladesh reported in 54 DLR 1 and accordingly the Customs authority will be bound to obtain direction form the National Board of Revenue on any question which appears to the Customs authority as discretionary exercise of power. Since we find that the National Board of Revenue has not yet formulated and imposed any condition, limitation and restriction under the Provision of Section 13(2) of Customs Act, 1969 we hold that by seeking direction in respect of granting bonded warehouse licence in fovour of the petitioner, the Respondent No.3 did not abdicate his power available un-der Section 13(1) of the Customs Act, 1969 to the Respondent No.2 National Board of Revenue rather the National Board of Revenue relying on unfounded matter directed the Respondent No.3 not to issue any further bond licence which cannot be maintained as lawful.

25. The petitioner on his second ground of objection further assailed the impugned refusal of granting bond licence on the ground of discrimination. Mr. Salahuddin Ahmed after taking us through the Annexure-D and D(1) categorically pointed out that the petitioner is victim of discriminatory attitude on the part of the customs authority since after the issuance of Annexure-c on 18.3.2003,. bond licence in favour of a competitor of the petitioner namely M/S.P.H.P. Steel Mills Limited has been issued on 25.1.2005. The learned Advocate pointing to the date of application of the petitioner, praying for bond licence, contends that since the petitioner also applied on 15.5.2005 the respondents are duty bound to treat the petitioner as standing on the same footing and accordingly grant the bond licence as prayed for.

26. We have perused the Annexures D and D(1) which are two bond licence granted in favour of M/S K.Y.C.R. Coil Ltd on 08.11.01 and P.H.P Steel Mills Limited on 25.1.2005. By cross referring these two bonds licence with Annexure-C we are unable to hold that the bond licence granted in favour on of M/S K.Y CR. Coil Ltd 08.11.2001 fall within the reference of Annexure-C but so far the bond licence granted in favour of M/S PHP Steel Limited on 25.1.2005 we find that since it was granted after the issuance of Annexure-C the petitioner is victim of discriminatory attitude on the part of the customs authority since M/S PHP Steel Limited is a competitor of the petitioner having the same industrial unit producing C.R.Coil.

<u>27. It further appears that Annexure C has taken into consideration the prospective Finance Act of 2003 and, aspired that the government on the basis of report of the revenue reforms committee will make control in respect of bonded warehouse licence and other related matters. From the Finance Act 2003, it appears, that the government amended the original provision of section 13 of the Customs Act, 1969 and conferred power on the National Board of Revenue to impose condition limitation and restriction upon granting of bonded warehouse licences. Therefore the aspiration as expressed in Annexure-C may be treated as has already been considered by the government and accordingly amended the provision of Customs Act. Therefore we have no hesitation to hold that refusal to grant bond licence for any industrial concern as mentioned in Annexure-H has no basis on the facts and circumstances prevailing. The customs authority since granted bonded ware-house licence to the other competitor of the petitioner and since the petitioner stands in the same footing of the other competitors, it is entitled to the grant of bond licence in relation of their imported goods including H.R. Coil.</u>

28. On assessment of the arguments made on behalf of the petitioner we feel that the petitioner successfully established his objection against the refusal in not granting bond licence in its favour and as such this rule deserves consideration.

<u>29. In the result the rule is made absolute. The refusal and non-granting of bonded ware-house licence in favour of the petitioner, through Annexure-B, is declared to have been made without lawful authority. The respondents are directed to grant bonded warehouse licence, as prayed by the petitioner through Annexure-E and El without delay if qualified on the prevailing practice.</u>

<u>However there shall be no order as to costs.</u>
